item.title: IDEA: ‘A web of canals and cobbled streets’: a city break in Haarlem in the Netherlands
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
It’s only 15 minutes away from the Dutch capital by train, but Haarlem feels a million miles from Amsterdam, and perhaps provides a more typical glimpse of the Netherlands than trailing around the well-worn tourist trail of Van Gogh, coffee shops and red lights. An attractive city of cobbled streets, gabled houses and canals, Haarlem is, as the Dutch would say, a gezellig sort of place – cosy, convivial, and full of intriguing nooks and corners. I’ve been coming here for years, and it seems odd that Haarlem is not better known, at least to UK visitors. This winter there’s the added draw of an exhibition devoted to the works of a local boy, the 17th-century painter Frans Hals, and his better-known contemporary Rembrandt in the city’s Frans Hals Museum (until 28 February 2027). No one really knows whether these two titans of the Dutch Golden Age of the 16th and 17th centuries ever met, but seeing their work hung together like this is powerful and compelling. The museum used to be the Oudemannenhuis (Old Men’s House), a retirement and care home where Hals lived out his final penniless years. The Hals-Rembrandt exhibition is perfectly in tune with Haarlem itself, in both its (relatively small) size and the historical insights it provides into the Golden Age. There are commissioned portraits of 17th-century merchant bigwigs, all beards, black gowns and ruffs, so-called tronies (portraits of ordinary people, including Hals’ informal paintings of fisherfolk, and Rembrandt’s sensitive, affecting study of his young son Titus) and both artists’ remarkable group portraits. A final room shows Rembrandt’s dynamic De Staalmeesters (The Wardens of the Amsterdam Clothmakers’ Guild) from the Rijksmuseum, alongside Hals’ depiction of the trustees of the Oudemannenhuis itself. Like many of the works in the rest of the museum, the faces in these paintings stare powerfully out at us from the 17th-century gloom. Above all, don’t miss Hals’ stirring and evocative Haarlem civil guard portraits of local militias, and a couple of 17th-century depictions of the city showing streets virtually indistinguishable from those you can explore today. Start exploring with a stroll to Peuzelaarsteeg, a nondescript street in itself, but where Hals is said to have had a studio, though there’s nothing here now apart from a graffitied image of one of his paintings. Afterwards, take a peek into the former home of the Cloveniers, the citizen militia or schutterij that Hals painted, on nearby Gasthuisstraat. Look for the two crossed muskets above the gate (part of it is now a municipal library). Walk from there through the pretty, ivy-draped streets of the Vijfhoek neighbourhood to the Proveniershuis, where an otherwise ordinary door opens on to perhaps the grandest of Haarlem’s many hidden courtyards – once the base of another schutterij. A crossbow over one of the doors gives it away. Hals was buried in the city’s magnificent Grote Kerk (Big Church). It’s like stepping into a 17th-century Dutch painting of a church interior: a vast, unadorned gothic space focused on a magnificent baroque organ at the western end: one of the largest in the world, and said to have been played by Handel and Mozart. The Grote Kerk is on the attractive Grote Markt (Big Square), flanked by cafes and restaurants, and the perfect point from which to launch yourself into Haarlem’s web of streets. Two minutes away is the Corrie Ten Boomhuis, where a family of Dutch Christians hid Jews and resistance fighters during the Nazi occupation – an alternative to Amsterdam’s Anne Frank House without the queues. Among several other museums worth seeing is Teylers Museum down by the river, a treasure chest of fossils, crystals, scientific instruments and late 19th-century Dutch paintings. It claims to be the country’s oldest museum, and its galleried, wood-panelled interior is alone worth the admission price. Perhaps the best thing to do is just amble and get lost: many of Haarlem’s historic streets look similar, with secret doors into sheltered courtyards or hofjes, and the streets are refreshingly free of global chains. There’s an excellent market on Grote Markt on Saturdays, and any number of stylish indie stores to browse in nearby, whether you’re looking for vintage clothes (Yenvi) or new ones (Stitch), chocolates at Pierre or Dutch liquorice at Dropje van Haarlem. Cyclists vastly outnumber cars in this city. Rent a bike (try Green Bikes by the train station) and head out to the Zuid Kennemerland national park, west of the city centre, a protected area of dunes, forests and lakes that gives way to the glorious sandy beaches of the North Sea coast. There’s no shortage of choice for great places to eat and drink. For breakfast or lunch, La Maru on Koningstraat is a great bakery, or try the sandwiches, salads and flammkuchen (sort of Dutch pizzas), at Meneer Frans in the historic centre. Alternatively, enjoy a pickled herring at the fish stall on Grote Markt. Another Haarlem pleasure is to stop off for a pils at one of its many cosy bars. Lively In den Uiver on Riviervismarkt – a typically Dutch “brown cafe”, housed in a former fish shop – offers a choice of 35 gins and 35 speciality beers. Or the Jopenkerk brewery tap, in a former church, is a five-minute walk from the Grote Markt. For dinner, there can be no more bizarre place than DeDakkas, in a greenhouse-like structure on the top of a multistorey car park near the river. It serves a sustainable, locally sourced menu, with superb views. There are plenty of places on Grote Markt to watch the world go by. Among the best is historic Grand Café Brinkmann. Or walk five minutes down Koningstraat to Botermarkt, on the edge of the Vijfhoek quarter, where Café De Roemer is one of a number of bar-restaurants with a covered terrace. Finally, there can be no better place to wake up in Haarlem than in one of the corner dual-aspect room at the 17-room ML hotel (doubles from about €119 room-only), right by the Grote Kerk, which has two good restaurants and a sleek bar. Across the road, the Amrâth Grand Hotel Frans Hals is a large, slightly cheaper alternative, while the Staats Hotel, on a quiet street two minutes from the station, offers cool, spacious and contemporary boutique rooms from €165 room-only, and also has its own bar and restaurant. The trip was provided by Netherlands Board of Tourism. Martin Dunford is one of the founders of the Rough Guides travel guide series and wrote the first editions of the Rough Guide to the Netherlands

item.title: IDEA: Seven travel trends that will define 2027
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
Seven travel trends that will define 2027 What do fantasy-inspired escapes, nostalgic holidays and a new kind of boys' trip have in common? They reveal how our changing attitudes to everything from technology to personal relationships are influencing where we go and what we want from our holidays. From seeking deeper connection to embracing otherworldly destinations, here are the seven travel trends to watch in 2027. Next year, travellers will increasingly be seeking out places that feel like another world, whether that's spectacular stargazing spots and ancient ruins or landscapes steeped in myth and folklore. According to Booking.com's 2027 travel predictions, 65% of travellers surveyed expressed interest in paranormal travel experiences, including haunted histories and supernatural encounters; while Pinterest Predicts 2026 noted a surge in searches related to mystical landscapes, with "Scotland Highland aesthetic" up 465% and "ethereal places" up 45%. Travel PR firm Lemongrass suggests that the growing popularity of "romantasy" fiction – which blends romance and fantasy – is helping fuel interest in these otherworldly escapes. But the appeal goes beyond beautiful scenery; it's about escaping the everyday and stepping into another world. "Everywhere we look in our cultural research, we see people seeking awe," says cultural futurist Jasmine Bina, CEO of Concept Bureau. "They want to feel connected to something bigger than themselves, to surrender to something that totally envelops them." Try it: Visit Zermatt, a Swiss Alpine village surrounded by dramatic peaks, considered by fans to be the real-life Velaris, the secret city in Sarah J Maas' A Court of Thorns and Roses series. The traditional boys' golf weekend is getting a makeover, with a new generation of group holidays challenging stereotypes about how men travel. According to Lemongrass' 2027 trends report, men's trips are seeing a growing focus on emotional wellbeing, with retreats designed to encourage connection, self-reflection and more open conversations about masculinity. Citing research from Bupa UK, the report notes that 50% of men have struggled with mental health difficulties, set against a backdrop of changing conversations around loneliness, burnout, work-life balance and financial uncertainty. Group trips can provide an opportunity for these discussions, as explorer Levison Wood notes in the report: "What I have learned is that men often speak most honestly when conversation is not the main purpose. They talk while walking, making camp, sharing food or dealing with a challenge together." "I see this trend growing, especially for men," says Bina. "Therapy and self-reflection have seeped into every part of life. We're at a point in culture right now where the definition and permissions of masculinity are greatly expanding." Try it: Both Sides Retreats offer men the chance to reconnect with their sense of purpose in the UK. In 2027, travellers are looking to recapture the carefree joy of childhood, swapping grown up responsibilities for the simple pleasures of being a kid again. According to Expedia, 57% of travellers surveyed are likely to book an "un-adulting" trip in 2027 – rising to 71% among Gen Z and millennials. Travel companies are responding with experiences designed to appeal to this sense of nostalgia and adventure. Walt Disney World has introduced an adults-only lounge at Epcot and offers late-night theme park events, while Universal Studios Japan has launched an adults-only Halloween Horror Nights overnight experience. Elsewhere, adults-only resorts and cruises promise care-free escapes where the practicalities are taken care of. "We increasingly see people having less shame and embracing the things they truly love," says Bina. "I see it less as shirking responsibilities and more about looking for extreme escape. When you talk to people that go on adult-only trips to theme parks, they'll tell you that those places make them feel safer and more optimistic, like there's order in the world again." Try it: Ride the waterslides at Jamaica's Princess Senses The Mangrove Resort, an adults-only all-inclusive resort with water-park access where you don't need to think about anything beyond having fun. As AI becomes part of everyday life, travellers are increasingly seeking something technology can't provide: human connection. While 40% of Americans now use AI for tasks such as travel planning, industry research suggests that shared experiences and meaningful interactions are becoming more important. According to Hilton's 2027 Trends Report, 60% of travellers surveyed are more drawn to water-based wellness activities when they can share them with others. Meanwhile, Skyscanner has seen a rise in large-group bookings. Human connection is worth paying for, says Priceline: in their recent survey, 66% of Americans said they would pay extra for exceptional personal attention. "Everything has become synthetic," says Bina. "Deepfake AI, bosses sending ChatGPT nonsense to their teams, misleading packaging – we are surrounded by the uncanny and the unreal. Connection is scarce, and in high demand." For a growing number of travellers, holidays aren't just about switching off; they're about discovering new interests and switching on your brain. While learning holidays are nothing new, the latest trend puts a greater emphasis on hobbies and the pleasure of play. According to Hilton, Gen Z travellers are nearly twice as likely as baby boomers to want to return home with a new interest they can continue pursuing, while holiday rental platform Vrbo has seen rising demand for "hobby hubs" – properties suited to everything from crafting retreats and photography weekends to antique hunting jaunts. "This is a really beautiful incarnation of our overall cultural shift toward play," says Bina. "Hobbies get us into our bodies and into flow states in a way that modern, commercialised wellness perhaps never could." Try it: Learn Spanish while walking the Camino de Santiago with Responsible Travel, combining mornings language lessons with afternoon hikes through northern Spain. The minibreak is getting even shorter. In 2027, travellers are increasingly embracing one-night getaways, whether it's to attend a concert or sporting event, celebrate a milestone or simply enjoy a quick escape. According to Hotels.com, 79% of travellers surveyed plan to book a one-night stay in the coming year, rising to 83% among Gen Z and millennials. Searches for one-night getaways have also increased by nearly 10% year on year. Dubbed "trip snacking", these bite-sized breaks offer a quick reset between holidays, with 71% of respondents saying they help tide them over until their next trip. Against a backdrop of rising living costs and economic uncertainty, the appeal of a shorter, potentially more affordable escape is easy to understand. "Short trips are part of a broader trend toward minification, like little treat culture, tiny homes and microweddings," says Bina. "It's economically driven but also well suited for peoples' increasingly busy lives. Smaller doesn't mean less – it actually means the opposite. When something is truncated, we need it to be that much more intense in order to satisfy our desires." Try it: Book a microbreak through Staycation, a platform offering hotels for 24 hours, 48 hours or even just a few hours across Europe. In 2027, the ultimate status symbol may be an experience that nobody else can replicate. From one-off cultural events to rare encounters with people and places, travellers are seeking one-of-a-kind experiences. FINN Partners calls this "unrepeatable travel", experiences whose value lie in their rarity and authenticity rather than their price tag. Bina says that this is all about how the idea of status is changing. "Columbia University professor Silvia Bellezza says we gain status in culture by creating distance from the norm, and for a long time, money was that distance," says Bina. "If you had enough money to travel to revered hotspots, your wealth equalled distance. But now that anybody can fake wealth on social media, money doesn't provide distance anymore. So the new status comes from unrepeatable experiences, a way of creating distance by the way of access and knowledge that nobody else has." Try it: Cruise the Nile during the total solar eclipse on 2 August 2027, when Luxor will be in the path of totality. Specialist voyages will bring travellers together with scientists and astronomers to witness the rare celestial event. – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: Diving the Sea of Cortez: What a Liveaboard Trip Really Looks Like
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Few places pack as much marine life into one stretch of water as the Sea of Cortez, the long arm of the Pacific between mainland Mexico and the Baja California peninsula. Day trips from shore reach only part of it. Remote seamounts, sea lion colonies, and protected reefs are often hours away by boat, so many divers choose a liveaboard. If you are thinking about booking one of the Nautilus Liveaboards diving trips in the Sea of Cortez, it helps to know what life on board is like, from the first briefing to the last night dive. Why the Sea of Cortez Is Worth a Liveaboard Jacques Cousteau famously called the Sea of Cortez "the world's aquarium," and the name still fits. Deep, nutrient-rich water rises along the Gulf's underwater ridges and feeds plankton, which then draws in everything from tiny reef fish to large pelagic species. A single week can include playful California sea lions, schooling jacks, mobula and eagle rays, moray eels, and nudibranchs. With some luck, you may also see hammerhead sharks, giant mantas, or whale sharks, depending on the season. Many of the best sites lie far from the main towns of La Paz and Cabo San Lucas. A liveaboard solves this: the boat moves while you eat and sleep, so every day starts at a new site instead of a long morning commute across open water. The rhythm of a liveaboard is simple, and most divers find it relaxing after a day or two. Days usually start early with coffee and a light snack before the first dive. The crew briefs you on the site layout, currents, depth limits, and animals you are likely to meet. Early dives often have the calmest surface conditions and the most active marine life, especially at seamounts where pelagic species gather. After a full breakfast and a surface interval, you do the second dive. Lunch follows, then time to rest, review photos, or watch the coastline from the sun deck. Surface intervals are part of the experience. Dolphins and even whales are sometimes seen from the boat between dives. An afternoon dive is often followed by a night dive, when the reef changes character. Octopuses hunt openly, crustaceans come out of hiding, and you may see bioluminescence. Nautilus advertises up to four dives daily, including night dives, depending on the itinerary and conditions. Divers ultimately choose how many they want to participate in. Every route is different, but a few experiences define diving in this region. - Sea lion encounters: At colonies such as Los Islotes* near Isla Espíritu Santo, young sea lions often swim right up to divers, twisting and blowing bubbles. For many people, it is the highlight of the trip. - Seamount diving: Offshore pinnacles like El Bajo are known for strong currents and big-animal sightings, including schooling hammerheads in season. - Wrecks: Several sunken vessels near La Paz have become artificial reefs covered in life, rewarding photographers. - Protected reefs: Marine parks such as Cabo Pulmo show what decades of protection can do, with dense fish populations and healthy hard coral. *Los Islotes closes to diving and snorkeling during the summer breeding season and typically reopens Sept. 1. Summer itineraries may visit other sea lion colonies instead. The main liveaboard season runs from summer into autumn, roughly July to November. Water temperatures in late summer can reach 29-30°C (mid-80s°F), and visibility is often 20-30 meters. Later in the season, the water cools, and visibility can drop, so check conditions for your dates. A 3mm wetsuit is usually enough at the warmest time of year. Bring a thicker suit or hood if you get cold easily or plan several dives a day. A surface marker buoy, reef-safe sunscreen, motion-sickness remedies, and a light jacket for windy evenings on deck are also worth packing. You don't need to be an expert to enjoy this kind of trip. Open Water certification and good buoyancy control are usually enough, since guides lead the dives and some sites, particularly inside national parks, require a guide anyway. More advanced divers will enjoy the current-swept seamounts and the chance to log many dives in a short time. Everyone gets the same advantages: little travel time, plenty of time in the water and a front-row seat to one of the richest marine ecosystems on the planet. A liveaboard in the Sea of Cortez is less about luxury than about immersion. You wake up next to remote islands, dive several times a day, share stories over dinner, and fall asleep while the boat heads to the next site. For divers who want to see the Gulf at its wildest, it is one of the most efficient and memorable ways to explore it. This story was published in partnership with Nautilus Adventures.

item.title: Minnesota’s Voyageurs National Park Named 2026 Dark Sky Place of the Year
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
For people living beneath the artificial glow of city lights, a sky filled with thousands of stars can seem like something out of science fiction. According to a recent National Park Service report, 80 percent of Americans cannot see the Milky Way from their homes. But at Minnesota’s Voyageurs National Park, a roughly five-hour drive from Minneapolis, some of the darkest skies in the country reveal the heavens in dazzling detail. And thanks to the park’s growing lineup of in-person and virtual programs, you don’t have to travel to the North Woods to experience the magic. This week, Voyageurs received one of the highest honors in conservation: DarkSky International’s 2026 Dark Sky Place of the Year award. The annual award honors individuals and organizations dedicated to protecting nighttime environments. “What makes this award so meaningful is that it isn’t about Voyageurs being a beautiful place to see the stars. We were certified as an International Dark Sky Park in 2020 for that,” Christina Hausman Rhode, executive director of Voyageurs Conservancy, its nonprofit partner of the park, told Outside. Since earning its International Dark Sky Park certification in 2020, Voyageurs has introduced some 8,300 students to the wonders overhead through its Virtual Dark Sky Classroom, welcomed nearly 6,000 people to Park After Dark and other nighttime programs, and drawn more than 1,300 visitors to six annual Star Parties. Add to that roughly 40,000 students nationwide who participate in Boreal Stargazing Week each year, and it’s clear the park’s reach extends well beyond its 218,000-acre boundary. This honor recognizes what has happened since, Rhode added: “A shared commitment by the National Park Service, Voyageurs Conservancy, and our gateway communities to protect these skies and share them with as many people as possible.“ Voyageurs also stands out because it’s about 40 percent water—covered by interconnected glacial lakes—a fact that adds to its stargazing prowess. Sweeping views are unobstructed by foothills, and its 30 calm lake surfaces act as mirrors reflecting the constellations and making the dark-sky experience all the more impressive. This is no Great Smoky Mountains National Park with its 12 million annual visitors either. With roughly 200,000 visitors each year, Voyageurs offers plenty of wide open space to take in the starscape. “Voyageurs doesn’t just protect some of the darkest skies remaining in North America,” Ruskin Hartley, CEO and executive director of DarkSky International, told Outside via email. “It’s the people behind that protection.” Hartley said that from the land managers and rangers to community partners, there’s a shared commitment at the park to preserve the night through responsible lighting, as well as to share the park’s wonders with the public. The recognition comes at the end of a particularly challenging year for wilderness conservation in northern Minnesota. In April, Congress passed and President Donald Trump signed a resolution that reversed a 20-year mining ban covering roughly 350 square miles of Superior National Forest near the neighboring Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. The move reopened the door to proposed copper and nickel mining operations. The threat to Voyageurs? Well, what happens in the Boundary Waters doesn’t necessarily stay in the Boundary Waters. The two protected landscapes are linked by the Rainy River watershed, a sprawling network of lakes, rivers, and wetlands. (Incidentally, the Boundary Waters and Voyageurs, along with Ontario’s Quetico Provincial Park, form one of the world’s largest dark-sky regions.) “Copper mining from a proposed Twin Metals mine would absolutely impact Voyageurs,” says Libby London, communications director for the nonprofit Save the Boundary Waters. Once pollution reaches the water, it can spread quickly for several hundred miles, explains Pete Marshall, communications director for Friends of the Boundary Waters Wilderness, another nonprofit organization that’s been advocating for the Boundary Waters area for 50 years. Governor Tim Walz signed an executive order in August to block the state from permitting copper mines in the watershed, but that order expires three months after Walz leaves office. In July, lightning-sparked wildfires fueled by hot and windy conditions forced the rare closure of Boundary’s entire million-acre wilderness, upending summer travel plans and prompting evacuations. Out of an abundance of caution, Voyageurs officials banned campfires and charcoal grills for six weeks. Against that backdrop, Voyageurs’ Dark Sky Place of the Year award is a welcome conservation victory. Protecting the night sky at Voyageurs has required more than simply keeping the lights off, of course. The park has had to rethink how it uses light in the first place. Under a new lighting management plan, outdoor fixtures were replaced with dark-sky-friendly alternatives that direct light downward rather than into the sky. National Park Service staff also began regularly visiting five locations throughout the park to measure the darkness using a sky quality meter, a device that measures the brightness of the night sky. On a scale where 22.0 represents the darkest natural night sky, Voyageurs averages an impressive 21.45—meaning that when the sun goes down, the stars really do come out. And while the award puts Voyageurs in the spotlight, the park’s greatest achievement may be what happens when the lights stay out. For Rhode and the Voyageurs Conservancy, the hope is that the recognition inspires others to look up—and take action.

item.title: Is an AI Data Center Coming to a National Park Near You? This New Map Shows Where.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
As America grapples with the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence data centers, two brothers have set out to map infrastructure project proposals nationwide—including those near public lands and national parks. Will Pattiz is the cofounder of More Than Just Parks, an independent public lands publication that tracks AI data centers. According to his research, at least 14 proposed data center projects are within ten miles of a national park boundary. His data also shows that 38 sites are planned within 25 miles of a national park, and 131 are within 50 miles. “The basic idea is that a lot of these [projects] are being done under the cloak of darkness or secrecy, and we want folks to know where they’re coming in and who’s building them,” Pattiz, a resident of Portland, Oregon, told Outside. “The stance that we take is that we don’t want them on public lands.” “Places like Utah, for example, have a huge amount of data center projects and some of the biggest ones that are being proposed,” Pattiz said. “Just depending on the size and scale, they take up a massive amount of resources and will have impacts on public lands one way or the other, whether it’s taking water or the land itself.” Data centers are rapidly popping up across the United States, fueled by the computing needs of artificial intelligence and cloud-based software. These centers house massive servers, data storage systems, and networking equipment, and they require sizable amounts of electricity and water to run and maintain the hardware. “The question that we want to see asked is: ‘What is the public benefit from this?’” Pattiz said. “So far, the ones that have been proposed on public lands, there’s no public benefit that’s been outlined.” To use Pattiz’s map, a user inputs their zip code, and the site shows the closest data center or proposed facility. The site then suggests how the center will affect utility costs, as well as the groups that support the center. “You can go through that discovery process yourself to decide whether you support [the center] or not, because these are things that are going to impact all of us, and you can decide where you land on that,” Pattiz said. The map auto-populates as more information becomes available. As of this writing, the tool reflects 2,086 data centers, 741 of which are still in the proposal phase. Of those, 77 are located within ten miles of protected land like national parks, wildlife refuges, and wilderness or conservation areas. Roughly half are in the American West. In Virginia, 97 data centers are proposed, and 12 are within 25 miles of Shenandoah National Park. At least 25 data centers are proposed in Indiana, according to the map, and eight are located within 25 miles of Indiana Dunes National Park. The map also includes several construction proposals that are extremely close to iconic National Park Service sites. Arizona alone has 26 active proposals, with three within 25 miles of a national park. In January, the City of Page sold roughly 500 acres to developers planning to build a $10 billion data center next to Horseshoe Bend, an iconic viewpoint along the Colorado River. The 500-acre parcel was previously protected for outdoor recreation. According to the City of Page, the proposal is undergoing public review and has not yet been formally adopted, but a planning and zoning meeting is scheduled for November 17. According to Pattiz’s map, the center is also located about five miles from the northeastern edge of Grand Canyon National Park near Lees Ferry. Just outside of Price, Utah, Pattiz found that a company called Valar Atomics applied for more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management land for data center buildouts, including permits for hundreds of small nuclear reactors, a fuel plant, and nuclear waste storage. According to a report published by NPR, the so-called Project Beehive would produce about 9.6 gigawatts of power for data centers. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces less than half of that on average, NPR reports. The land is . Located about 40 miles from Zion National Park, Antelope Data Center is slated for development as part of a 640-acre, 1.5-gigawatt project that will include an on-site natural gas power plant, according to The Salt Lake Tribune. The Iron County Commission approved a conditional use permit in June 2026. Large-scale data center rollouts represent an inflection point in American history, Pattiz said. As construction crews have erected these centers, they have become political lightning rods in American towns and cities. Pattiz believes that giving Americans transparent, readily available information about where big tech is breaking ground will help them track what developers are building in their backyards. “At the end of the day, data is data,” he added. “Whether or not there’s a need for these things is a totally separate question from where they’re being built and what impact they’re going to have on you and the places that you love.”

item.title: A Woman Was Swept Off an Oregon Beach and Left Clinging to Rocks Offshore. A Lifeguard Rescued Her in the Darkness.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Rocky sea stacks rise along Oregon’s southern coast, where a woman was swept into the ocean by massive waves at Secret Beach on November 8. (Photo: Juan Pablo Jim/Getty) A woman was rescued from the ocean after powerful waves swept her off a beach in southern Oregon on November 8, leaving her clinging to rocks offshore as darkness fell. The woman had been walking along Secret Beach, a secluded stretch of rocky coastline roughly 20 miles north of the California border, when a swell pulled her into the ocean, according to a statement posted to Facebook by Curry County Aquatic Safety. Unable to reach her, the woman’s husband called 911 around 5:18 P.M. The report did not name the woman. When a Curry County sheriff’s deputy arrived at the scene, the woman had been swept 200 feet down the coastline, where she was stranded on rocks roughly 50 to 70 feet offshore. “People want to come see the waves, and we have a lot of great scenic viewpoints for them,” Luke Martinez, an aquatic safety officer and lifeguard with Curry County Aquatic Safety, told Outside. “Unfortunately, people sometimes get stuck in bad spots, and that was the case Sunday night.” The National Weather Service had issued a high surf warning for Oregon’s southern coast that day, forecasting breaking waves of 25 to 33 feet. Martinez told Outside that he and fellow lifeguard Shannon Ingram responded to the emergency as large waves continued crashing onto the beach. “It was pretty unruly,” Martinez said. “There was huge surf. The tide was out, and we couldn’t see much, but there were surges occurring up and down the beach.” Ingram reached the shoreline ahead of Martinez just after sunset. Wearing a wetsuit and a safety helmet, she determined she could safely enter the churning water and made her way to the stranded woman. She checked her for injuries, secured her with a rescue tube, and brought her back to shore. The woman was able to walk off the beach with assistance before being taken to a hospital for further evaluation. “It was a good ending to something that could have been pretty bad,” Martinez said. Secret Beach sits along the Samuel H. Boardman State Scenic Corridor, a 12-mile stretch of coastline dotted with rocky cliffs, secluded beaches, and offshore rock formations. Martinez noted that the area has surged in popularity due to social media, even though its rugged geography poses serious risks. “We live along a really rugged coastline,” Martinez said. “It’s similar to people visiting the mountains and climbing 14ers. Not everybody realizes the dangers involved.” Curry County Aquatic Safety has just two lifeguards—Martinez and Ingram—covering roughly 100 miles of coastline and several rivers. On November 8, they spent much of the day advising beachgoers about the unusually powerful surf, emphasizing that volatile conditions can catch people off guard before help can arrive. “Beachgoers will be watching the smaller waves, thinking they understand how far the water is reaching up the beach,” Martinez explained. “Then that longer-period swell arrives and surges much farther up the beach than the waves they’ve been watching. During these events, our beaches can become dangerous for anybody, including experienced surfers or swimmers.” Massive waves are a recurring hazard along the Pacific coast from October through March, when winter storms generate the largest swells, according to the state of Oregon. During major storms, offshore waves can exceed 30 feet. Also on November 8, videos captured similar scenes elsewhere along the coast. Footage from Cannon Beach showed a young girl nearly being swept into the ocean, while another video from Winchester Bay showed two people scrambling to escape incoming waves as their dog was swept into the water. The dog was later rescued. Another round of massive surf is expected to batter the Oregon coastline in mid-November. A National Weather Service warning projects breaking waves reaching 30 to 35 feet November 13 and 14. The agency is urging visitors to stay off beaches, rocks, jetties, and piers while the high swells continue.

item.title: REVIEW: Wine: A Global History by Kathleen Burk — the drink that shaped civilisation
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink
Wine: A Global History by Kathleen Burk — the drink that shaped civilisation Following eight millennia of grape expectations, from ancient rituals and royal excess to prohibition, mass production and changing modern tastes For 8,000 years, writes Kathleen Burk, “wine has been a drink, a libation, a medicine and a commodity”. For millennia, it has been seen as “a gift of the gods”, with grapes being turned “apparently by magic” into a substance that can change the world for those who drink it. What greater pleasures are there, she asks, “than sharing a bottle of wine with friends”? The author, a distinguished historian as well as an oenophile, has combined her twin passions to write a sweeping, masterful account of the role that wine has played around the world. For starters, wine made life better for all our ancestors — it was safer than water, thanks to the fact the process of fermentation kills off harmful bacteria. That was not what King Jamshid, the mythical ancient Persian ruler traditionally credited with the discovery of wine, thought. He was so upset when his beloved grapes spoiled that he placed them in a jar labelled “poison” — which was drunk by a woman in his harem whose terrible headaches were promptly cured. One of the stories that Burk weaves through Wine: A Global History is how vines and wine spread — along the silk routes into the Hunza Valley in modern-day Pakistan, as far as Japan, into lands conquered by the Romans, and later into the Americas by the Spanish, and to South Africa, Australia and New Zealand by the British. Or there was North America, which was referred to by Scandinavian settlers around 1,000 years ago as “Vinland” for a reason — namely the “vines heavy with grapes” — but then saw a series of planting booms after the arrival of later Europeans: by the start of the 20th century, wine was being grown in 43 of the then 48 states. Not long after, alcohol was being referred to as “the curse of the working man”, with the result that winemakers had to look on as hundreds of thousands of gallons were flushed into the gutter. Prohibition was another chapter in views about alcohol — and wine in particular — that could be ambivalent. A drunken argument in Medina led to wine being frowned on in Islam though not, as Burk notes, banned: after all, she notes, wine was greatly enjoyed in Arabia and was often consumed in legendary quantities — especially by caliphs who liked to enjoy themselves. They were not the only ones. We learn of King Zhou, the last ruler of the Shang dynasty 3,000 years ago, who “filled a large pool with wine and ordered groups of men and women to chase each other in it naked”. That sort of thing would have appalled Emperor Charlemagne, who, apart from having an aversion to “see anyone drunk, and especially himself and his own household”, was either something of a hygiene freak or had friends who were. During his reign (771-814), instructions were sent out that demanded that anyone involved in making wine should pay “the greatest attention to cleanliness” and should make sure to wash their hands — and to use wine presses rather than their feet. The health-and-safety directives of more than a millennium ago are an example of the sorts of nuggets that can be found in the book. Another is the Gallo brothers of California who built up an empire on the back of Julio telling his brother Ernesto “I’ll make all the wine you can sell” while the latter promised to “sell all the wine you can make”. Burk introduces superstar wine connoisseurs like Steven Spurrier and Robert Parker as well as their ancient Roman counterpart, Pliny the Elder, who knew and loved his wines. We find out about Greek wine being shipped to Burgundy and about the investment in vineyards in Ukraine, Moldova, Croatia and elsewhere. In a nice touch, Burk starts each chapter with a wine suggestion: I’ll be giving a Lebanese red called the Gaston Hochar, Château Musar 1999 a go before long. She ends on a sober note. The modern age has been good for wine, with a proliferation of blogs, newsletters and discussion groups helping foster conversations and recommendations. But, the author notes, “the future of wine is uncertain”. While the young are embracing new trends, including orange wine, there is also alcohol-free wine — Burk ponders if that even counts as wine. There has been a marked fall in recent years with consumption down by 12 per cent since 2007. In China, home to more than half the world’s varieties of grapes — as well as to a class of super-rich who had bought quality and quantity since the turn of the century — wine sales went down by almost 25 per cent in 2023 alone, presumably because of economic pressures and the fear of being seen to be overindulging. Wine drinking, as Burk notes, “is too pleasurable to give up”. Cheers to that. Wine: A Global History by Kathleen Burk Profile £30/Basic Books $40, 640 pages Peter Frankopan is Professor of Global History at the University of Oxford Join our online book group on Facebook at FT Books Café and follow FT Weekend on Instagram, Bluesky and X

item.title: UPDATE: Grand Canyon hotels set to reopen after flash flooding: What to know if you’re visiting soon
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Editorial note: The Grand Canyon Lodges inside the park at the South Rim are projected to reopen on Nov. 20, 2026. Phantom Ranch inside the Canyon is expected to remain closed through January 2027. For updates on the Transcanyon Waterline and hiking trails, check the official national park alert page. A deadly flash flood swept through Grand Canyon National Park in northern Arizona over the weekend. An active search-and-rescue operation is underway along the Colorado River, and parts of the inner canyon and South Rim are closed at this time. Due to extreme damage and flash flooding in the Grand Canyon this past weekend, the National Park Service announced immediate closures of the following areas until further notice: Phantom Ranch, Phantom Ranch cabins and canteen and Bright Angel Campground. The entire North Kaibab Trail — from the North Kaibab Trailhead to Phantom Ranch — is also closed until further notice. The Silver and Black footbridges crossing the river have been affected as well. For the latest trail and closure information, visit the park's Key Hiking Messages webpage. A threat of severe weather still remains, and visitors are urged to exercise caution. Videos posted online by the Associated Press showed the destruction caused by the flooding. This devastating flash flood comes just a year after the Dragon Bravo wildfire forced the evacuation and closure of the North Rim in July 2025. The closure of the inner canyon will allow the National Park Service and the Arizona Department of Public Safety to continue search-and-rescue operations. There are still visitors unaccounted for, and the NPS Investigative Services Branch is seeking the public’s assistance. The flash flood significantly affected infrastructure in the canyon, including the Transcanyon Waterline, and, as a result, the visitor facilities at the South Rim are also affected. Is it safe to travel to Grand Canyon National Park? Yes, it is safe to travel to portions of Grand Canyon National Park, but there are some restrictions that visitors should be aware of. We suggest bookmarking the park's main page, which lists updates and links to advisories. The Places To Go page is full of helpful visitor information and maps. South Rim hotels projected to reopen November 20 The National Park Service has issued a closure notice for Monday, Aug. 31, at noon local time for the South Rim hotels located within Grand Canyon National Park due to damage to the Transcanyon Waterline. All water at the South Rim is delivered via the waterline, and additional reserves are running low. Only dry camping will be permitted at the South Rim. It’s important to note that the park will remain open for day use, and food-and-beverage services at the South Rim will remain open (though some may reduce hours of operation). As we’ve previously reported, the Transcanyon Waterline dates back to the 1960s, and the park has already invested $208 million in a multiyear rehabilitation project that isn't expected to be completed until 2027. The most recent update provided by Grand Canyon Lodges lists the hotels at the South Rim as projected to reopen on November 20, 2026. Town of Tusayan hotels remain unaffected Tusayan is the gateway to the South Rim of Grand Canyon National Park at the Route 64 entrance, and its hotels and restaurants remain fully operational and unaffected, as it's located outside the national park. What to know if you have a Colorado River rafting trip scheduled Until further notice, the Colorado River is closed to river traffic due to metal structures and debris entering the river, according to a notice from the National Park Service. River operations rangers are coordinating with visitors already in the canyon, and the Grand Canyon River Alert system is also sending advisories. If you have an upcoming river trip scheduled, you should contact the commercial outfitter that you booked with or the NPS River Permits office for trip-specific information. TPG has a comprehensive guide to credit cards that covers trip cancellation and interruption, including what might be covered in the event of a natural disaster. Our hearts go out to those affected by the flooding at the Grand Canyon. If you have a trip planned soon, be sure to double-check the location of your reservation to see if your trip is affected so you can take appropriate steps to reroute or rebook. The most recent updates and advisories will be posted on the park's official website. For updated information on the status of hiking trails and facilities at Grand Canyon National Park, visit the park’s Plan Your Visit page.

item.title: JSX brings semi-private flights to Boston with 2 new routes
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
JSX is bringing its popular semi-private flights to Beantown. The boutique air carrier plans to begin flying from Boston this winter, JSX said this week. The company's service will be based out of the nearby Laurence G. Hanscom Field (BED) in the town of Bedford, Massachusetts. The Boston service will launch with a route to New York City on Feb. 8, followed by flights to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport (OPF) in Florida beginning on Feb. 11. JSX will operate four daily flights between Boston and New York from Monday through Friday, with two flights on Saturday and three on Sunday. The Miami service will run once per day five times a week: Monday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Notably, JSX did not specify which New York airport would host the Boston flights. A spokesperson did not immediately answer TPG’s request for further details. JSX typically flies to New York’s Teterboro Airport (TEB) and Westchester County Airport (HPN), although various restrictions set by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey mean that JSX cannot publicly promote TEB as a destination. Because of those restrictions, anyone looking to fly to or from New York has to sign up for the free Club JSX program, which offers rewards and has no minimum spending or flying requirements. Passengers can also earn United MileagePlus miles under a partnership between the two companies. The carrier will use its Embraer E145 aircraft on both routes, which can seat up to 30 passengers in a 1-1 configuration. Fares start at $199 one-way between Boston and New York, with one-way flights between Boston and Miami starting at $599. “Greater Boston represents an exciting new chapter for JSX, marking our first entry into Massachusetts and an important milestone in the continued expansion of our East Coast network,” JSX CEO Alex Wilcox said in a statement. “As one of the nation's leading centers for business, innovation, and higher education, Greater Boston is a natural fit for our unique approach to flying,” he added. How JSX makes private-jet convenience available to the public JSX operates as a “hop-on charter” service, which essentially operates private charter flights that anyone can buy a seat on. It means that JSX flights operate more like private flights than commercial, using posh private Fixed-Base Operators (FBOs) instead of public airport terminals and allowing passengers to venture from curb to seat in just 20 minutes. The flight experience itself is equally luxurious with no middle seats, lots of legroom, Starlink Wi-Fi, complimentary snacks and drinks and checked luggage that’s returned right at the side of the plane. Overall, the service pitches the idea of private jet convenience for a fraction of the cost. The public charter service — which does not bill itself as an “airline,” due to different regulations between charter carriers and public airlines — operates out of 29 airports across the U.S. and Mexico. Although private jet passengers typically bypass TSA screening, JSX implemented a more thorough in-house screening process in 2025 to address security concerns. Still, the process is remarkably quicker than going through the public terminal, making JSX an appealing option for those looking to skip the hassle of a regular flight. JSX's flights from Boston are already on sale, with service scheduled to start in February. With the entry to New England, JSX adds its 29th city, and brings its own entry to the competitive business of moving premium travelers between Boston and New York. Related reading:

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Pecan Cream Pie With Brown Sugar Custard
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Inspired by the towering Praline Pecan Pie served at Das Dutchman Essenhaus in Middlebury, Indiana, this pecan cream pie brings together the best parts of pecan pie and cream pie. A gooey, nut-packed base sits beneath silky brown sugar custard and a pillow of whipped cream, with crunchy candied pecans scattered over the top. It’s a lot of pie—in the best possible way. The pecan layer is jammed full of butter-toasted nuts, but the secret ingredient is a dollop of sour cream, which helps prevent crystallization and keeps the filling from becoming overly sweet. More sour cream goes into the whipped topping, adding tang and helping it hold its shape. Dark brown sugar and plenty of vanilla give the custard its toffee-like flavor. This is admittedly more involved than a classic pecan pie, but the work is straightforward and easy to spread over a couple of days, making this a particularly good project to tackle before Thanksgiving Day. Toast the pecans once for both the gooey filling and crunchy topping, and make the crust and pecan layer ahead so all that’s left is the custard, whipped cream, and a little patience while everything chills. What size pie pan should I use? Use a standard 9" metal pie pan. Metal promotes even browning and can accommodate more filling than a standard glass or ceramic dish of the same diameter. This is a generously filled pie, so pan capacity matters. Can I make pecan cream pie ahead of time? Yes. You can bake the crust and pecan layer up to one day ahead and store them, covered, at room temperature. Once you’ve added the custard, the pie needs at least four hours in the refrigerator to set. The fully assembled pie can also be refrigerated for up to one day. For the crunchiest topping, scatter the candied pecans over the whipped cream just before serving. How do I know when the brown sugar custard is thick enough? The custard should start to bubble, then become glossy and thick like pudding as you stir it over medium heat. This generally takes 3–4 minutes. Don’t rely on refrigeration alone to thicken it: The cornstarch needs to cook sufficiently on the stovetop for the custard to set properly. Keep stirring to prevent lumps or curdling. - Total Time 2 hours (plus 6 hours for chilling) Need to make a substitution? - CrustStep 1Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until combined (mixture will be very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center; pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead dough in bowl a couple of times to bring together (some dry bits may remain). Step 2Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface; dust top of dough with rice flour or all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed. Pat into a ½"-thick disk; wrap in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours. Step 3Place racks in upper and lower thirds of oven; preheat to 425°. Let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap and roll out on a lightly floured surface to a ¼"–⅛"-thick round. Wrap around rolling pin; transfer to a standard 9"-diameter pie dish (preferably metal). Unfurl into dish, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into dish. Trim overhang to 1". Fold overhang under and crimp edges as desired. Prick bottom and sides of dough in several places with a fork. Freeze 15 minutes. Step 4Crumple up 2 sheets of parchment paper; smooth out and place over dough. Fill dish with pie weights or dried beans. Set pan on a foil-lined baking sheet and bake crust on lower rack, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are golden brown and bottom is opaque, 35–40 minutes. Remove from oven; reduce oven temperature to 350°. Lift parchment and weights out of pan. - Pecan Layer and Nut ToppingStep 5While the crust is baking, whisk 2 large eggs, ⅔ cup (packed; 133 g) dark brown sugar, and remaining 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl. Set egg mixture aside to use for the candied pecan topping and the pie filling. Step 6Melt remaining 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium saucepan set over medium. Add 2½ cups (300 g) raw pecans and cook, stirring gently, until nuts are slightly darkened in color and fragrant, 5–7 minutes. Pour through a fine-mesh sieve set over a small bowl, reserving both the pecans and the browned butter. (You’ll use the same pan to make the custard; no need to wash it.) Step 7Transfer ½ cup toasted pecans to another small bowl to make the topping: Add 1 Tbsp. reserved egg mixture and toss to coat. Spread on a parchment-lined baking sheet and bake on upper rack until dry to the touch and a honeycomb-like texture appears on surface, about 5 minutes. Let candied nuts cool. Step 8For the filling: Finely chop remaining toasted pecans and add to the remaining egg mixture along with the reserved browned butter, 2 Tbsp. sour cream, and 1 tsp. vanilla extract. Stir to combine. Scrape into crust and bake on lower rack until pecan layer is mostly set but still jiggles slightly in the center when gently shaken, 15–18 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack; let cool until barely warm, at least 30 minutes. Do Ahead: Candied pecan topping can be made 3 days ahead; store airtight at room temperature. Crust with pecan layer can be baked 1 day ahead; store, covered with foil, at room temperature. - CustardStep 9Heat 1½ cups heavy cream and 1 cup whole milk in the same saucepan you used for the nuts over medium until steaming, about 2 minutes. Step 10Meanwhile, whisk 6 large egg yolks, ¾ cup (packed; 150 g) dark brown sugar, ⅓ cup (40 g) cornstarch, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ cup whole milk in a medium bowl. Step 11Gradually pour warm cream mixture into egg mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Pour mixture back into pan and cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, until it starts to bubble, then becomes glossy and thick (like pudding), 3–4 minutes. Scrape into a medium bowl, add 6 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 4 tsp. vanilla extract, and whisk until butter is melted and custard is emulsified. Cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Let custard stand at room temperature while the pecan layer cools. The pecan layer can still be slightly warm when you add the custard; neither needs to cool completely. Step 12Uncover custard; whisk until smooth. Spoon over gooey pecan layer, spreading evenly to edges. Cover and chill at least 4 hours and up to 1 day. - AssemblyStep 13Whisk ¼ cup sour cream, 3 Tbsp. powdered sugar, remaining 1 tsp. vanilla extract, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 cup heavy cream in a medium bowl to medium peaks. Spoon over custard and spread into an even layer. Break candied pecans into large pieces and scatter on top. Do Ahead: Pie can be assembled 1 day ahead. Chill. Editor’s note: Originally published in October 2025, this recipe has been updated to clarify the recommended pan size and instructions. The ingredients and tested techniques remain unchanged.
