item.title: REVIEW: The new London restaurants to try in November 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
We've always got one eye on any new restaurants opening on the London food scene. Our editors are on the ball for the latest openings in each London neighbourhood, from Covent Garden restaurants to Shoreditch hotspots. For the ultimate list of places to eat in the city, check out our definitive guide to London's best restaurants. These are the places that we consider the crème de la crème, from generations-old spots that have stood the test of time and Michelin-starred dining rooms that get better each year to mind-blowing new openings from this list that we decided deserved a spot on the ultimate round-up of the best restaurants in London. For new restaurants opening in London recently, we've seen follow-ups from some of the city's biggest-name chefs and a handful of restaurant openings that have stopped us in our tracks: from London's newfound love for BBQ to a Turkish restaurant that's turning heads. These are our favourite openings of the past six months. How we choose the tastiest new restaurant openings in London The best new restaurants in London are the most exciting places to eat that have just opened in the capital city. Ranging from small affairs with daily changing menus from up-and-coming chefs to Michelin-starred spots with fresh new menus, these are London's new restaurants we've got our eye on right now. Every restaurant on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has eaten at that restaurant. When choosing new restaurants, our editors consider both high-end and affordable eateries that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for stand-out dishes, a great location, warm service, and serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new restaurants open in London. Best new London restaurants in November 2026 Following the devastating fire that destroyed beloved Endo at the Rotunda in September 2025, a hole has been left in London’s dining scene ever since. So, when news of Endo Chelsea broke, it may come as no surprise that securing one of the 10 seats in the intimate omakase felt akin to getting your hands on Glastonbury tickets. The new West London outpost is darker and sexier yet distinctly more traditional than its predecessor at the Rotunda. Inspired by the sushi counters of the 1920s and 30s, the atmosphere is theatrical and practically electric as we wait for the star of the show to appear. I take my seat, sip my delicious tea-infused Negroni, and watch as the seamlessly choreographed 19-course performance unfolds. Undoubtedly, Endo is the star of this show, handing each guest a piece of sushi and swapping tales at the same time. From the beautifully ornate sake cups, designed and handcrafted by Endo himself, to the three varieties of rice used throughout the omakase, each paying homage to one of his great teachers. The food is, unsurprisingly, exceptional. Local produce meets Japanese technique. Much of tonight’s fish comes from Cornwall, where Endo recently lived and worked alongside local fishermen. Highlights include langoustine nigiri, turbot and mackerel, alongside an oyster paired with a cup of exceptional 200-year-old discontinued sake. Then there’s the Wagyu with cep mushroom and chive. Three hours slip past in the blink of an eye. A triumphant new chapter, this new opening is like a phoenix rising from the ashes. Welcome to the new church of Endo. Lucy Bruton Address: 8-9 Blacklands Terrace, London SW3 2SP This isn’t just a new restaurant to try in London, Lunette is the new restaurant in London. The debut solo restaurant of chef Florence Knight, previously of Sessions Art Club and Polpetto, has all the hallmarks of an A-list haunt. There’s the swishy address – squirrelled down a 10th-floor corridor and up some glossy stairs within St. Clement, the first hotel from Soho House founder Nick Jones since he stepped back from the private members’ club. There’s design-showroom good looks in the long dining room with purposefully incongruous tables: steel rectangles, glossy round tables and a cream sofa seating area in the middle for the truly brave. And then of course, the million-pound Thames views with an outdoor terrace that is destined to have its own waitlist come summer. Rare for these seen-and-be-seen spots, though, the food is actually great. So phenomenal, in fact, I found myself scraping every last morsel and sliver of sauce from each plate. The four-course lunch and six-course supper menu is plainly worded but is anything but. Runner bean, squid and yarrow translates to a bright green bowl of fresh herby magic. Equally dazzling is the marigold orange of the cock crab, pepper and yolk, a lick-the-plate-clean egg-jammy, buttery risotto with a footnote of peppery heat. I was sceptical of the custard, onion and caviar, with the latter ingredient often used so haphazardly that it lost all appeal. This is where Knight’s restraint really shines – the caviar is respectfully the star rather than a hedonistic afterthought. There’s a masterful light and shade with each dish, along with the option for wine pairings to really hit the high notes. If you go it alone, most bottles of wine are under £100, which is refreshing. Likewise, the £16 signature martini is poured in two servings into the daintiest glasses. With two pudding courses, I left full, happy and wondering how long it will take until a Michelin star comes calling. Lauren Burvill Address: 180, The Thames, 12 Temple Place, Temple, London WC2R 2NF I must admit, I never thought a hole-in-the-wall this charming could exist a few steps from London’s chaotic Strand. But on a gloomy work night, when I walked into this new bistro housed in an old church furniture workshop, it felt like the place had been here for decades. The comfort food here is straight out of a French farmhouse, with a subtle British touch. It’s all bursting with flavour, with portions large enough to satisfy you, while leaving room for the next course. We start off our evening with a one-bite raw beef croustade dusted with comté and, because I can never get enough of my favourite French cheese, moved on to a tarragon-topped comté quiche that I know will become a post-work staple. The mains are French classics that weave in local fare (think stuffed cabbage chou farci but with pigeon); we opt for delectable grilled mackerel in a rich lobster bisque, and what might officially be one of my top three comfort dishes in London: the hen of the woods (a sponge-sized nutty mushroom that grows around oak trees) and armagnac vol-au-vent with sauce Parisienne. I grew up with my mother making vol-au-vent, so enjoying a forest-y twist on such a nostalgic dish was a treat. For dessert we shared an unbeatable chocolate mousse drizzled with olive oil and sprinkled with flaky salt, and one of my favourite French desserts: black fig clafoutis. For those unfamiliar, this eggy, crustless tart typically uses whole cherries, so not having to worry about the pits with this version was a win-win. Tamara Southward Address: 42 Maiden Lane, Covent Garden, WC2E 7LJ It’s not often I find myself dining at the same restaurant twice in one week, but The Horses is such a hot ticket right now that it’s no surprise when one of my more switched-on foodie friends excitedly tells me that she’s booked us lunch there a few days after my first visit. And I have no problem returning – this latest outpost from Public House Group (The Hart in Marylebone, The Pelican in Notting Hill) hits all their signatures: top-drawer UK produce, served simply and beautifully, in an elevated homage to the great British pub. The Horses dates back to 1790, and has been revamped by PHC with a traditional pub on the ground floor and three levels of seafood dining on top, a nod to the former Smithfield fish market nearby. Downstairs is heaving when we arrive on Friday night, but escaping up a back staircase we enter into the relative calm of the dinky oyster bar. There’s a subtle sea theme running through the design, with limewashed ceilings, soft curtains reminiscent of sails or netting, orb lights hung with chains, and an ice-packed treasure chest of crustaceans overseeing it all from the horseshoe-shaped counter bar. It’s candlelit, intimate and wonderfully romantic. The chatty staff have a genuine enthusiasm for seafood – we get tips on which order to eat the oysters, freshly shucked in front of us, and whether they need a drop of homemade chilli sauce or mignonette. The cod’s roe on smoked bread is basically fancy taramasalata on toast and a fantastic pub snack, but the standout starters are the clams and cockles in a creamy, cider-y broth and the moreish squid coated in fried pastry crumbs with chilli mayo. Among the mains, the fish is the thing – there are six to choose from, plus specials, and six sauces to mix and match (“they’re actually all free right now, so I’d just go mad,” murmurs our waitress). Monkfish with langoustine gravy is satisfyingly meaty, and John Dory with the surprising recommendation of peppercorn sauce really works; but the star is the Dover Sole with garlic butter, accompanied by a pile of new potatoes studded generously with garlic, and sea greens. It all feels special but not stiffly formal, and I’ll be back yet again for pub snacks and pints in the near future. Olivia Squire As a Notting Hill resident with the luck of a job that’s given me dibs on newly opened restaurants, being at the centre of the anticipation is always exciting. But the lead-up to Nakimushi opening its doors felt quieter, as if those who’d caught a glimpse wanted to keep the place a secret immediately. On the affordable end compared to its sister restaurant Eel, Nakimushi is the marriage of Urchin and Robin’s Ramen – two former London residencies that now see chefs Yuji Shimokawa and Robin Kosuge bring opposite ends of Japanese cuisine together. We share wild hamachi with nori oil, vegetable ohitashi worth it for the mushrooms alone, and a tuna summer roll with blackberry and hibiscus (my favourite). For our mains, we choose lobster ramen with sobrassada and pistachio matcha ramen with daikon cress. If the veggie broth at a restaurant is this decadent (not to mention, healing), it’s a winner in my opinion. The ground floor is communal-style, where you watch your food being prepped in an open kitchen from counter seating or a shared table. But weave up the Scandi-style stairwell and you’re in a proper dining room, whose timber walls are covered with cool contemporary art and bottles of Japanese whisky. There’s only one dessert on the menu, the mugi-cha creme caramel; the only area I’d like to see revisited. It’s good, but perhaps not enough to warrant single status. Tamara Southward Romy Gill has been a permanent fixture on the London food scene for more than a decade. Since the unfortunate 2019 closure of her first restaurant, Romy’s Kitchen, in South Gloucestershire, Romy has become a welcome sight on TV screens between the release of three cookbooks – the latest being Romy Gill's India: Recipes from Home, in 2024. Being such a household name, you’d be forgiven for being surprised that her new venture, Romy Gill at The Pem, is the chef’s first restaurant in six years. It’s the aforementioned cookbook that greets us as we pass over the threshold, after weaving through Conrad London St. James, into a fantastically crimson dining space. Privacy panels divide the restaurant's heart into booth hideouts that feel more intimate than the sprawling space they’re set in, while tables along each side offer corners where besotted foodies feast under subdued lamplight. Cocktails arrive, the taste of cumin curiously coating my palate as I sip on the Malhar, crafted with Amrut Single Malt and homemade cumin syrup – the Anarkali isn’t to my taste, but a Negroni obsessive’s dream, I’m sure. Starters land and the feast begins as we pluck decoratively presented king prawns (and king they are) from their heads and savour melt-in-the-mouth tandoori lamb chops. The highlight, however, is the samosa chaat; a crisp samosa topped with chickpeas, sev, pomegranate seeds and yoghurt in a sensational jumble of taste and texture that we long to do all over again. Heaps of rice and chunks of torn naan, fresh out of the charcoal tandoor, come into action, soaking up the sweet butter chicken sauce before our waiter performatively surrounds the hake moilee in a refreshing, vibrant curry leaf broth. After initial insistence that we need no dessert, we cave and coat sugar-dusted churros in a decadent chocolate sauce – a perfectly gluttonous finish, after all, to a warming meal that ushers us gently into the autumn months. Connor Sturges Address: Romy Gill at The Pem, 22-28 Broadway, London SW1H 0BH Best new London restaurants in September 2026 There’s something ever so cool about anonymity, and as I walked straight past the door of Kid in Soho, I had to remind myself of this. There are no signs, bells or whistles here, just a rusty brown door with an almost imperceptible goat symbol marked on it. Kid holds a quiet, understated vibe that oozes confidence – and rightly so. The hotly anticipated restaurant is the latest project from former Mangal II chef Sertaç Dirik, who’s teamed up with David Carter of London mainstays Oma, Agora and Smokestak, making it quite the force to be reckoned with. Inside, the vibe is dimly lit, with exposed brick and a bustling open kitchen, reaching far beyond what the subtle exterior might at first suggest. The menu, meanwhile, is Turkish-inspired but with plenty of twists, blending a lovely mix of soul-soothing, comforting classics with an elevated execution. Highlights included the balloon-like tombik pide (worth visiting for alone), a smoked aubergine dip topped with whisker-thin grains, and the İçli Köfte – the most sumptuous ball of dry-aged beef, juicy and flavoursome, that will be living in my mind rent-free for a while. Of course, most customers opt for the namesake shoulder of goat on the menu, served in a huge traditional clay pot and slow-cooked overnight for the ultimate fall-away meat. Interestingly, the wine list is ordered not just by region, but by when wine-making practices first began in each destination. We opted for a light Cypriot glass to match the restaurant's tone and offset some of the richer dishes. So, is the new kid on the block actually worth the hype? I’d say yes – and I’d even hazard a guess that this new dining address has some seriously long-standing appeal. Lucy Bruton Address: Kid, 53-55 Frith Street, London W1D 4SJ One could be forgiven for thinking this rather enviable London postcode – on W1S’s Cork Street – can be a little pretentious at times. But that’s certainly not the case at Bar Finch. Perusing the menu prior to arrival, I felt – dare I say – a touch underwhelmed. Burgers and chips, Caesar salad, roast chicken; you know the drill. But that’s not the case either. What you actually get when you patter down the steps is a new, polished neighbourhood go-to that feels akin to plopping yourself down in a very chic living room, complete with terribly friendly staff and the cheerful spirit of a proper Italian bacaro. Ashy wood panelling and lashings of texture keep things cosy, while great slabs of marble wherever you look remind you that you’re still firmly in Mayfair. Suitably settled in our plush leather booth, we got stuck in. The menu, a triumph of Italian-tinged comfort food, now makes sense. Portion sizes are perfect for sharing (and actually so – not just billed that way on the menu only to arrive disappointingly tiny). The hand-rolled pastas were most popular among fellow diners, arriving tossed in silky, slow-cooked ragù, while a tomato salad and a side of beans tasted as fresh as anything you’ll eat all week. The steak has a delightfully indulgent thread of marbling that rivals the tabletops, and proper crispy chips, but the dish to order is the chicken piccata – complete with a salty, crackling skin curled up pleasingly at the edges and a generous smattering of oily capers for good measure. Drinks pairings are treated with equal flair. There’s a curated wine list featuring both indie Italian winemakers and classic European vintages, but you won’t feel shortchanged if you skip them all and go straight for the cocktails, which are far too good to miss. All the Italian classics are present, but the standout – promptly earning a second order – was the Champs-Élysées; bright with lemon and Green Chartreuse, given a grown-up edge with a hit of cognac. Whatever you do, don’t leave without ordering the tiramisu, which is utterly huge (so don’t say you weren’t warned). Make sure to leave room, as taking leftovers home isn’t allowed. But who cares, in any case? This is a delightful spot to hunker down on a cold and gloomy evening at leisure. There’s no need to rush away so soon. Charley Ward At the start of September, husband-and-wife team Gabriel Waterhouse and Patricia Wakaimba opened the doors to Waterhouse, a much-anticipated restaurant, wine bar and garden set inside a Victorian warehouse on buzzing cobbled Ezra Street, just off Columbia Road Flower Market. Following the closure of The Water House Project in June, their new home is an impeccably designed space, flowing from raised beds outside, where the chefs pick fresh herbs, into a bar area with stainless steel countertops and handcrafted oak furniture, and through to the dining room, which serves 24 covers in an intimate nightly sitting. The food measures up to the space. Chef Gabriel draws on his Northumberland upbringing and the region’s traditional cooking techniques, while adding a playful touch with in-house ingredients such as miso, koji and garums. Start with a punchy, syrupy fig leaf martini at the bar before embarking on the 11-course tasting menu. The ensemble hits a high note immediately with a rich, comforting cep and Madeira tea, before moving into bites that challenge the palate while remaining comforting and, ultimately, delicious. The courses balance refreshing zing, like the oyster with cucumber and sorrel, with familiar but elevated mouthfuls, like the moreish onion crumpet. Larger plates, including a smoked haddock porridge (oyster mushroom for vegetarians), hit a hearty note. The meal ended on singing hinnies, a traditional griddle cake, with boozy-forward lavender and Laphroaig cream. If you manage to have some room left, the seasonal cheese selection isn’t to be missed. This is a savoury, umami-rich tasting menu that has immediately risen to the top of my list for celebratory meals. The team have nailed the difficult task of creating fine-dining plates without a stuffy atmosphere. Gabriel and Patricia’s history of supper clubs, where their journey began, can still be felt in the environment they’ve curated at Waterhouse. Chloe Laws Queen's Park is having a little moment in the limelight of late, preening and showing off as curious eyes turn its way thanks to a slate of clever openings (Don't Tell Dad, where a queue forms for glossy cinnamon buns and plump pains au chocolat every morning; The Salusbury, a smart pub with a dining room that punches above its weight; Naples-inspired joint Casa Felicia) joining some long-standing favourites like Harry and Meghan's favourite Italian Ida and brewery Wolf Pack. Now, everyone's talking about a wine bar that's taking interiors inspiration from Spaghetti Westerns and looking to four imaginary muses – the writer, the actor, the architect and the director – to pull together its cellar book. The Bar Blondie site used to be Milk Beach, an Antipodean all-day restaurant which kickstarted the Queen's Park foodie revolution eight or so years ago. The space is still owned by Aussie Elliot Milne, who's given it a tip-to-toe renovation. Interiors, designed by Macaulay Sinclair (also behind Dishoom's Permit Room and Hawksmoor, among others), are now mid-century sexy with a masculine edge: nutty woods, dark greens, art curated by The Other Art Fair founder Ryan Stanier. The menu looks to France and Italy: delicate grilled artichokes with pecorino di fossa and honey and silky Cantabrian anchovies in puddles of Provençal olive oil are perfect to share, while heartier pastas (we especially liked the paccheri alla vodka with nduja) are the smart choice if you're settling in for the evening. Award-winning sommelier Alexandra Price has curated a wine list that celebrates everything from well-known, beloved estates to emerging producers. I visited earlier in the summer, on opening night, but live close enough to confirm that the buzz has sustained into autumn, too – this is a smart Act II for a cosy neighbourhood joint. Sarah James Best new London restaurants in August 2026 Chef Aktar Islam is something of a Brummie legend. He was the first British-born Bangladeshi chef to be awarded a Michelin star in 2019, just one year after opening his debut restaurant, Opheem, in Birmingham's Jewellery Quarter. A few years later, Opheem became the joint-first Indian restaurant to receive two stars, alongside London's Gymkhana, in the 2024 ceremony. Opheem's status as the city's go-to Special Occasion table to book is firmly cemented. So when news of Islam opening in London reached me, a native Brummie, I was naturally a) very proud (how often do chefs find success outside of London and then transplant to Zone 1?) and b) desperate to get through the door. And it is quite the door. Oudh 1772, Islam's Borough restaurant, is set across a Grade-II listed Victorian townhouse, where each storey sits sort of wonkily on top of the next. That's not to say it's not beautiful: designer Polina Sychova collaborated with Islam on the soft, sumptuously layered spaces – all curvy arches and thick drapes, peppered with antiques from Lucknow and even a bespoke hand-painted ceiling in the attic bar. Rather than bouncing across the Indian subcontinent, Islam's menu focuses on the flavours of Awadh, a historic region in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh. Regional street food is a playful place to start: chaat with white peas and potato or gol guppa (better known here, perhaps, as pani puri) are crispy and best eaten with your hands, a perfect way to start any evening. We boldly take on the mutanjan dum biryani with oxtail, a king prawn kebab and the Awadhi monkfish curry – be warned that while this might certainly be a white tablecloth sort of establishment, the portions are hearty. They're also, luckily, all perfectly pitched – perfumed biryani, garlicky prawns, creamy curry. Like Opheem before it, this is undoubtedly somewhere for a properly nice supper – prevented from ever becoming too proper by the friendly team and Islam's plucky menu. Add it to the list for your own next Special Occasion. Sarah James Address: 66 Union Street, London SE1 1TD Somewhat unexpectedly located above The Globe Tavern, a buzzy pub on the corner of Borough Market, is Kismet. After passing a throng of pint drinkers, visitors climb a winding staircase and enter a Turkish meyhane – a traditional tavern known for live music and family-style meals. Kismet has captured that atmosphere perfectly: dark, glittering mahogany benches, delicate lace curtains and vintage photographs make the restaurant feel wonderfully homely. Turkish music bubbles away in the background, with live performances on the qanun, a traditional string instrument, even hosted every Thursday evening. The menu follows Turkish meyhane cooking, so come prepared to share. Start with Atom, a thick buffalo milk yoghurt topped with chilli butter; cool and tangy against the gentle heat, it is particularly good scooped up with bread or piled onto Sigara Böreği, a crisp pastry filled with salty white cheese. From the charcoal grill comes Tavuk Şiş, smoky chicken thigh with red pepper, alongside Patates Kizartmasi, fried Cyprus potatoes. Wash it all down with Basketcase, a bottled lager brewed in partnership with Coalition Brewery, or, my personal favourite, a glass of raki. The Turkish anise-flavoured spirit is made for sipping alongside food, its clean, herbal finish acting as a refreshing palate cleanser between bites. The final flourish comes with dessert, when waiters glide between tables carrying silver trays above their heads. Lowered on request, they reveal rows of Turkish tea in delicate tulip-shaped glasses and slices of pistachio baklava drowned in syrup. Kismet is only a year-long residency in the space, so visit while you can. Amelia Dhuga Address: Upstairs at The Globe Tavern, 8 Bedale Street, London, SE1 9AL Cue Point is determinedly not a newcomer to the London restaurant scene. For a decade, the hybrid Afghan-Texas BBQ of Kabul-born chef Mursal Saiq and head chef Joshua Moroney has been making a name for itself through pop-ups, residencies and stints at breweries. This summer, they've finally found a permanent home for their low-n-slow, fired-up cooking. Cue Point at The Garden Bar is set inside an unchic West London boozer with, as the name hints, a truly enormous garden out back. Here, meat – Wagyu brisket, oak-smoked lamb shank, black lime pepper chicken bites – is smoked to meltiness, or else cooked over licking flames. Saiq's immaculate Afghan flavours are anything but shy and retiring, and a perfect match for Moroney's expert BBQ techniques. Those chicken bites' gnarly exteriors give way to soft meat – we boldly paired ours with the smoked pimento garlic chilli cheese flatbread to start. Wagyu brisket steak served with fluffy Texas naan and cowboy butter is a non-negotiable, although we'd also recommend ordering the flaky chilli-citrus seabass for something a little (emphasis on the word) lighter. The sticky toffee pudding with Bertotti kulfi was a surprise standout: moreish and sweet, Saiq works with West London gelataria Bertotti to perfect the kulfi. The team serve a special menu on Sundays, when Saiq tells me that people try to sneak in the door; advance reservations are so hard to get. This is West London's opening of the summer, and a must-book for anyone seeking serious flavour. Sarah James Address: Garden Bar Grill & Smokehouse at 41 Bramley Road, Notting Hill, London, W10 6SZ It's been 20 years since chef Adam Byatt opened Trinity, which in restaurant years is practically ancient. In that time, the Clapham Old Town spot has not only survived but thrived, earning a Michelin star and cementing itself as a south London favourite – its signature beef tartare is still one of the best dishes I’ve ever had, and I don’t even like beef tartare. So when Byatt opened his latest table, Italian-inspired Rosina, in Wandsworth Common, it was busy from day dot. Busy but effortlessly breezy, with smart couples seated at white linen tables adorned with plates of bread, lemons and olives, and single white candlesticks. Antipasti comes to the table with a vibrant flurry – crimson tuna crudo, smoked sardines on toast, and a heavenly bowl of rainbow Datterini tomatoes with basil, nectarine and buffalo mozzarella. This is the kind of place where everything is confidently simple, and the bread basket is put to good use mopping up every sauce and vinaigrette. For mains, a pillowy turbot is roasted on the bone and swimming in lemon, capers, parsley and wilted spinach. The intriguingly named ‘post-service pasta’ was my favourite; an understated yet masterful bowl of spaghetti with anchovy, chilli, garlic and parsley, essentially the dish Byatt likes to make for himself after a shift in the kitchen. Wonderfully oily and crunchy in equal measure, I ate every tiny crumb and noodle. Pudding is served from the marble trolley that holds court in the centre of the restaurant, with tiramisu rustically served with a generous dollop tableside. If there’s room to try two, the not-too-sweet but cheese-heavy Rosina's torte is a worthy option; the torte and the restaurant are named after Byatt’s daughter Rosie, who also works in the kitchen. Lauren Burvill Address: Rosina, 35 Bellevue Road, London SW17 7EF I visited All Roads during one of London's many 2026 heatwaves, so it says something about how delicious the food is that I wasn't remotely overwhelmed by the plates of mac and cheese, lamb from the house pot or fried wings that were placed in front of me on one of the hottest days of the year. While the rest of London was digging into light salads, or maybe a barbecue, I was more than happy to get stuck into the hearty dishes from chefs and partners Malika Green and Paschelle Brown, who have finally put down roots in Brixton following three years of sold-out supper clubs. The menu blends Caribbean cuisine with British, European and Southern American influences, resulting in a list of dishes that are hearty, moreish and full of flavour. Split into snacks, smalls, grill and plates (with just two or three dishes to each), it's tempting to order the whole menu – take three friends, and you probably could. Unfortunately for me, I was with just one friend, so we had to be discerning (albeit still rather greedy). Having tried over half of the menu, I truly think it would be difficult to order badly here, but my favourites were undoubtedly the chilli parm clams, served in a sweet and salty tomatoey-soy sauce, with crispy pancetta and topped with parmesan, or the impossibly cheesy baked mac and cheese. We ordered a fresh tomato salad to break up the dishes, and ended with homemade sorrel cheesecake ice cream. In the end, despite the heat, there's nowhere I'd rather have been on a Wednesday evening than here in Brixton Village, soaking up the vibe, flavours and fun of this memorable new spot. Abigail Malbon Address: 44 Atlantic Road, London SW9 8JN After earning a fiercely loyal following during his two-year residency at All My Friends, chef Man Hon Luk's first bricks-and-mortar restaurant – in the spot formerly occupied by Silo above Crate Brewery – was a natural next step. I never made it to the pop-up, but just knowing that Hon perfected his craft at world-renowned, Michelin-starred Interstellar BBQ was reason enough to clear the diary, hotfoot it over to Hackney Wick and see what all the fuss was about. The space is cool, casual and buzzing – high ceilings, whitewashed walls and simple red wooden tables and chairs let the food do the talking. Hon’s cooking is clearly shaped by his time in Texas, but what lands in front of us is something entirely his own: smoky, low-and-slow meats elevated with Chinese flavours and techniques. Every bite melts in your mouth, with just the right hit of spice and sweetness and the kind of deep caramelised crispy bits you’d fight your fellow diner for. The beef short ribs with Sichuan peppercorn sauce are the star of the show (tender, peppery and sticky) but don’t sleep on the sides; perfectly crunchy green beans with an umami-rich glaze, and a silky mac and cheese with a tangy mustard-laced sauce. Our only regret? Opting to share a bowl of the creamy mango coconut pudding – one each is a must. Sarah Allard Address: First floor, Unit 7, The White Building, Queen's Yard, London E9 5EN Best new London restaurants in July 2026 When Jackson Boxer opens a new London restaurant, it’s safe to assume it’ll be a smash hit. The chef and restaurateur behind buzzy Brunswick House, Dove and Henri has just opened a new neighbourhood spot on Exmouth Market. Interiors are industrial, with bare brick walls, a metal bar in the centre and curtains hiding candle-lit tables in intimate corners. There’s also plenty of tables that spill onto the sun-drenched street. We dined at Vesper a full month after opening, as tables really are that hard to come by. We made sure to book an early 6pm reservation, as the infamous burger you may have seen plastered all over your Instagram, often quoted as one of the best burgers in London, is ordered off-menu to 10 lucky customers on a first-come, first-served basis. We secured the fourth burger of the evening. The bun is covered in sweet glaze, hugging a hefty slab of seared and torched beef with a rare centre, layered with caramelised onions and oozing gorgonzola sauce. We’d recommend sharing, or you’ll be rolling home without a chance to try any of the other delicious plates. Our favourite dish of the night was the fried potato pizzette: a little circular pizza bread topped with pineapple, stringy stracciatella cheese and mortadella. Other highlights include the green bean salad coated in goat's cheese and gooseberry tahini, the chicken agnolotti – al dente pasta pockets bursting with fragrant chicken liver in a madeira jus. For pudding, order the punchy poached apricot flavoured with ginger and amaretto. Plates were scraped clean, as were our little gimlets, previously filled with the Vesper martini finished with a little squirt of citrus oil. Sophie Knight Address: 8-10 Exmouth Market, London EC1R 4QA Italian seafood restaurant group Langosteria has a knack for attaching itself to smart addresses in glamorous European locations, from Milan's Design District to St Moritz and the waves at Paraggi near Portofino. So it’s no surprise that the Milanese group’s first UK outpost has made a beeline for Raffles London at The OWO. Whitehall's neoclassical Portland stone grandeur doesn't quite evoke the summery spirit of the Ligurian Riviera, but once you pass through its doors, you're transported to that familiar Langosteria world, with its signature animated wallpaper and matching ambience. Here, everything is bold and impactful with a touch of experimentation – including the bar cocktails. From the concise list, the Pomodoro Mezcal, a smoky take on a Bloody Mary, confused my vodka receptors, but the Spicy Margarita with jalapeño was the unequivocal star. Food-wise, Langosteria casts a wide net in pursuit of freshness and quality, hauling its catch from Italy, Spain, France and Scotland. Locavore advocates will scream, but the quality is undeniable. My Sicilian red prawn starter – butter-soft and topped with wafer-thin slices of pecorino – was beautiful. The mains included Langosteria classics like the King Crab Special Edition 2007 and the Brittany Lobster "Spicy Blue”; I plumped for the crispy-skinned black grouper Chateaubriand, its saltiness offset by tangy-sweet caponata (Sicilian aubergine, olive and caper relish). My langoustine with lobster in a puddle of zingy lemon butter was perfectly al dente, but the Milanese turbot with asparagus and saffron proved somewhat immemorable. I chased it all with a glass of Ferrari Brut from a wine list that features most of the Champagne heavy hitters alongside an impressive, Italian-dominant selection of reds and whites. Portions are generous throughout, and for guests of the Raffles hotel, it's just a short stagger to their rooms upstairs. Noo Saro-Wiwa Address: Langosteria, Whitehall Place at The OWO, London, SW1A 2BD At the back of The Cadogan, A Belmond Hotel, is an elegant wooden staircase that King Edward VII (when he was the Prince of Wales) ascended to visit his lover, the Victorian actress and socialite Lillie Langtry. It still stands as a testament to the history (and discretion) of this particular 1880s Chelsea townhouse, and today, though less steeped in scandal, it is as regal and luxurious as ever. The Cadogan is also home to Willett’s, a new British bistro that seems set to become a hotspot in its own right, even amongst those not staying upstairs. Studio Shayne Brady, the interiors team behind the renovation, has modernised while remaining true to the hotel's history – bathing the space in calming blues and greens. Executive chef Michael Turner (a Gordon Ramsay alum) is producing à la carte dishes that showcase the very best of British produce in unfussy, delicious dishes. The sourdough crumpets with gentleman’s relish and dressed Dorset crab were the definite showstoppers and are destined to become signature dishes. Mini but mighty, I’d have been more than happy with plates of those alone. Seasonality and locality are buzzwords thrown around quite loosely these days, but Willett’s really does do credit to everything that is brilliant about the produce of the British Isles. I'd also recommend the succulent Beef Wellington and the Colchester oysters. We’ve no doubt that this restaurant will become as legendary as some of the hotel’s historic residents. Cass Farrar Address: 75 Sloane Street, London, SW1X 9SG Devotees of all things Stateside were intrigued when one of America's best cocktail bars, New York City's Dante, jumped across the pond in 2025 to pop up at grand dame Claridge’s. Rather than tire and bloat at yet another cross-Atlantic collab, the gourmands kept coming. And so, a year later, the hotel restaurant closed its doors for a facelift any Mayfair resident of a certain age would approve of, led by Bryan O’Sullivan Studio, with a fresh palette of green-and-blue tones and fantastical, botanical murals by Beth Rodway, to welcome Dante as a permanent resident of the neighbourhood's slickest hotel. We follow Billecart-Salmon Champagne with a taster of the Negroni Rosa, a watermelon concoction that tastes like a swig of the summer to come. A host of NYC favourites are now on the menu – we sample delicate caviar tarts and champagne pearls and are taken aback by the gargantuan grilled king prawns, their smoky, chilli-butter scent enveloping our booth. If a dish is preceded by the restaurant’s name, you know it’s one the chef’s hedging their bets on. And so the Dante smash burger arrives: a juicy patty coated in provolone cheese and topped with sweet caramelised onion, beside perfectly crispy chips awaiting their saucy demise. Burger devoured and Parmigiano Reggiano-doused veal Milanese inhaled between us, we call on our second stomachs for pudding with a side of spectacle. An espresso martini arrives, my face staring back at me in cocoa dusting courtesy of the bar’s cocktail-printing sorcery, alongside an uber-indulgent sticky toffee doughnut that illuminates our woozy cheeks with a whiskey flambé. It's a fiery finish to a meal I’ll be dining out on for a long time to come. Connor Sturges Address: Dante Mayfair, Claridge's, Brook Street, London W1K 4HR Best new London restaurants in June 2026 When we walk into Pavilion Road’s The Sea, The Sea – already a familiar name in Chelsea, but now a restaurant serving far more than just drinks and oysters – we don’t know what to expect. Above the ground-floor raw bar, tables are bathed in light, and the design is minimalist, but we quickly learn that all attention is poured into the fare. The menu spotlights lesser-known fish, plus whatever catch is locally abundant from the seafood suppliers they've built trusted relationships with. We start with cold sake and a tin of Imperial (as a caviar enthusiast, I love that the sour cream comes pre-topped with chives), followed by butter-soft Isle of Skye scallops with flowering currant. Often, the raw bar usually outshines everything else to me, but three warm dishes – cuttlefish ragu with green almond, smoked Chalkstream trout on a Jersey royal mash, and a rice vinegar-steeped John Dory with maitake – are impossible to top. The ragu is nothing like we imagine: no pasta, just clean-cut cuttlefish with an unbelievably flavourful squid ink salsify that results in an immediate repeat order. Come dessert, don’t look beyond the potato ice cream with smoked eel. It sounds hard to wrap your head around, and for that reason, you must order it. Tamara Southward Address: 243 Pavilion Road, London SW1X 0AW A new opening in Mayfair comes with glitzy high expectations, which we immediately felt as we were swept through the doors of MA/NA by a suave-suited doorman. He guided us through the long, winding bar space with a house DJ and down to our table under huge bonsais and gold statement lighting. A martini is poured table-side as we browse the extensive menu divided into small plates, robata (meats from the Japanese grill), sushi, steak cuts and large plates. We ordered to share: rock shrimp tempura in a glazed sticky sauce, juicy chicken thigh skewers from the robata grill, a 12-piece sushi platter with fresh cuts as selected by the chef (which could also pass as a piece of art) and the crunchy duck salad with sweet pomegranate. But, our favourite dish, which – fair warning – comes with a big price tag, was the Japanese A5 Wagyu slices served on a hot Himalayan salt stone, which not only flavours, but sears the meat from its heat. Melt-in-the-mouth slices of the finest beef, packed with flavour. MA/NA is on par, if not tastier than some of London's favourite high-end Japanese spots, with equally flashy guests and interiors. Sophie Knight Address: 30 Upper Grosvenor Street, London, W1K 7PH 14 years since its New York debut, chef Jody Williams has brought Buvette (and with it, the spirit of the West Village) to the cobbled streets of Covent Garden – slap bang in the middle of Neal's Yard. This charmingly chic bistro – complete with curated antiques and a black bicycle parked out front – somehow manages to strike just the right balance between familiar and fancy, with a day-to-night menu focusing on locally-sourced produce. We start with a crisp glass of bubbles as we make our selection, following the house suggestion of sharing three to five dishes between two. Plates are indulgent yet remarkably delicate; a vibrant ratatouille, fresh steak tartare, garlicky escargot, and decadent dauphinois. The standout is, unsurprisingly, Buvette's signature croques; we opted for the forestier, a vegetarian riff on the original, paired with a generous pour of white wine (French, naturally). To end, tarte tatin and a mousse au chocolat, followed by a perfectly chilled martini made just the way you like – a highlight among the well-executed classic cocktails on offer. I can’t wait to visit again, whether for a flaky morning croissant and espresso or another evening encounter with that croque... Drew Burns Address: Buvette London, 2 Neal's Yard, London WC2H 9DP Foodies and film fanatics flocked to Lupa when it opened its doors in Highbury – an Italian feeding frenzy from restaurateur Ed Templeton and chef Naz Hassan, fuelled by The Gentleman star Theo James’ involvement. The reviews were promising, and bookings soon became hard to come by, so it came as no surprise when the trio announced a follow-up – Ornella. On the corner of a leafy suburban street in London Fields, this new arrival is an edible love letter to Milanese fare that the capital’s food scene has long been crying out for, named in honour of the late singer Ornella Vanoni. Inside, it’s simultaneously cosy and sexy, diners tucked into banquettes and huddled around circular tables illuminated by flickering candlelight. Proceedings start over punchy sbagliato and caffè amaro cocktails – easy on those, mind – before the fluffiest focaccia in town arrives, warm and doused in glittering olive oil, alongside wafer-thin slivers of salty mortadella and coppa. There’s a choice of four starters – shoutout to the sea bream tartare, I hear, from my companion – followed by five ‘primi’ dishes. We slurp on salty onion broth and twirl our forks to catch shavings of cheese in the simple yet moreish butter and Parmesan tagliatelle, all washed down with generous pours of Venetian Manzoni Bianco. Naturally, onto secondi, a satisfyingly crisp chicken Milanese, used mostly to mop up heaps of silky mashed potatoes that likely contain more butter than potatoes (no complaints from us). We saunter into the night, hands in circular motions on our stomachs, remarking on how beige and calorific our spread became. No regrets at all, mind, as we plot our return to get snug in one of Ornella’s corners when the mercury drops, if not before. Connor Sturges Address: Ornella, 51 Wilton Way, London E8 1BG It’s no small feat bringing Italian summers to London, so it comes as no surprise to any Italophile that Francesco Mazzei is the one leading this charge for the foodie moment that’s taken root within the grand dame walls of London’s Corinthia Hotel. Designed to transport, its namesake and menu are inspired by the southern regions of Italy, where the sun is the most intense at midday, translated as ‘Mezzogiorno’. Personally more accustomed to London’s shades of grey, I was surprised to enter the opulent Northall bar and find myself in a nonna-esque open kitchen that doubles as a walk-through to the main restaurant. Here, a communal oval table sits opposite the kitchen, where an intimate group sit watching folds of dough being expertly handcrafted into pasta and breadsticks by the chefs in their whites. Inspired by the Baroque palazzos of Southern Italy, the restaurant is adorned with custom-made Murano chandeliers hanging from tall ceilings, held up by dramatic pillars adjoined to a waffled terracotta ceiling, which makes me think of a gelato cone. The scene here on a Tuesday evening is mostly out-of-town pals sharing plates, business comrades and on this occasion, a Hollywood A-lister, but the winning majority here were couples holding hands across tables and huddled in booths. We start by nibbling on the longest breadsticks I’ve ever seen - simple and all unique, the only concern is filling up on them, but they are surprisingly light. Next comes an injection of colour with the Pipi Cruski Limone Di Rocca Mayo, a traditional dish of fire-red peppers that are fried and best enjoyed slovenly dipped into lemon butter. Despite the colour, these aren’t spicy and have the most excellent crunch. Among the tables, we tuck into an antipasti of Orkney scallops, which are tender but fragrant alongside Batutta Di Manzo Inglese, a refreshing mix of chopped beef, salad leaves, pomegranate seeds and large shavings of black truffle. Mouths still full but contentedly chatting, it’s easy to see the inspiration behind this place. With excellent company and ambience, come and come again, but definitely share the hand-made pasta with native blue lobster sauce and T-bone among the table, while you snack on humble traditional Sicilian vegetables and of course, an entire bowl of zucchini sticks. To finish, the showstopping Tiramisu is necessary - presented to the table in a family-style bowl, the friendly server affectionately spoons the dessert onto our plates, like they are welcoming us to the family. Megan Wilkes Address: Whitehall Place, London, SW1A 2BD, United Kingdom Website: corinthia.com/en-gb/london/mezzogiorno/ Slap-bang in the heart of Soho, Kumori is a 30-seat handroll bar where most of the action happens at the counter, creating an intimate, immersive feel. Inside, the space feels a little like stepping into a spaceship – all brushed-metal surfaces and iridescent pink and purple lighting. From the plump made-to-order handrolls to the carefully curated soundtrack, everything about Kumori feels cool, fresh and considered. Knees brush as we pore over the tick-box menu, leaving me spiralling as I weigh up how many of the handrolls I can reasonably fit in; there are simply too many good options. The cocktail list is an equally delicious debate, eventually landing on a yuzu mezcal margarita and sitting back to settle in for the show. Behind the counter, chefs move with speed and precision through a menu curated by head chef John Randy De Guzman (formerly Nobu, Tobi Masa and Katsuya). Each roll is served from chef to patron the moment it’s made, turning dinner into a kind of live theatre. Lucy Bruton Address: Kumori, 26 Denman Street, London W1D 7HX

item.title: REVIEW: Where to eat in south London, by restaurateur James Dye
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink
Where to eat in south London, by restaurateur James Dye The co-founder of One Club Row and Bambi shares his go-to neighbourhood spots This article is part of FT Globetrotter’s guide to London When I was growing up in New Cross in the 2000s, there were lots of music venues and pubs but very little in the way of good neighbourhood restaurants — the sort of place everyone wishes they lived or worked within walking distance of. So back then it was a lot of trips to the East End or West End. That has massively changed over the past 15 years. South-east London now has everything, from Michelin-starred places in Camberwell and London Bridge to brilliant neighbourhood joints perfect for every occasion, from first dates and milestone celebrations to far more ordinary evenings. Top marks for the establishments where the proprietor knows your name; even better if the bartenders know your favourite drink. The list that follows is made up of the local spots I’ve found myself returning to time and time again, places that feel perfectly familiar and comforting, yet transport you somewhere else. 40 Maltby Street (London Bridge) In a city where a hot new restaurant seems to open every other day, it’s easy to forget about the classics. Not 40 Maltby Street, though. I have been to this picturesque wine bar under the arches of London Bridge station a lot — it is easily some of the best cooking in London. I have enjoyed everything from light summer lunches at one of the highly coveted tables outside through to long winter dinners with trains rumbling overhead. There are normally beautiful cheeses, fritters made with seasonal vegetables (think asparagus in the spring and pumpkin in the autumn), a brilliant salt cod brandade, expertly cooked fish and, of course, fantastic low-intervention wines courtesy of Gergovie Wines (the wine importer it shares the railway arches with). Open Wednesday, 5.30pm-9pm; Thursday-Saturday, noon-3pm and 5.30pm-9.30pm. No reservations. Website; Directions Brunswick House (Vauxhall) My old mate Frank Boxer, who owns Brunswick House with his brother Jackson Boxer, once said he measured how much he liked a friend’s restaurants by how jealous he was of not owning them. Well, I’ve never told him, but I’m a little jealous of Brunswick House. This antique-filled Grade II-listed Georgian mansion sits defiantly in Vauxhall surrounded by steel and glass skyscrapers, but inside you will find incredible interiors courtesy of architectural salvage company LASCCO (which the restaurant shares the building with) and fantastic creative, ingredient-led, seasonal cooking courtesy of Jackson and his team. My favourite memory was having the after-party for my wedding here. My Dad was playing in the cellar with his jazz band and I got a little carried away and welcomed a couple of wedding crashers from the restaurant, thinking they were long-lost family. My wife was not impressed when we got the wedding pictures back and the first picture was of my newly acquired friends. Though I’ll forever be thankful for the late-night Ogleshield cheese toasties at our wedding, and other food highlights include excellent homemade breads, beautiful crudos, wood-fired John Dory and the occasional Negroni on their terrace. Open Tuesday, 6pm-9.45pm; Wednesday-Saturday, noon-2.30pm and 6pm-9.45pm; Sunday, noon-3.45pm (5pm for drinks). Website; Directions Hausu (Peckham) One of the most rewarding things in hospitality is watching people who have worked for you go on to open their own restaurants, with great success. Hausu is my favourite. Opened two years ago by brother and sister duo Holly and Tom Middleton-Joseph alongside Christian Williams, it’s the perfect neighbourhood restaurant. You can have a few snacks at the counter while you watch Holly cooking over live fire in the open kitchen, go for a long dinner in the restaurant with a few friends or pop into the cocktail bar on the first floor for drinks and a hi-fidelity music programme. It has amazing music, great drinks, creative food and a spirit of fun that is so often lacking in restaurants these days. Recent standouts are the XO Orkney scallop with seaweed, Merinda tomato fritti and salt cod with tomato vine aioli. Drinks-wise, ask Tom and his team for a recommendation from their eclectic cocktail list — we’re talking the likes of the Salted Iberiko Tomato Martini or the Mezcal & Sesame Old Fashioned. You won’t be disappointed. Open Tuesday-Friday, 5pm-10pm; Saturday, noon-10pm; Sunday, noon-4pm. Website; Directions Trinco (East Dulwich) The mark of a great neighbourhood restaurant is how they treat solo diners and one of my favourite memories was a solo lunch at Trinco shortly before my daughter was born, a glass of wine and book in hand, knowing this might be the last quiet moment I had to myself for a while. Not only is the service amazing, it’s actually a restaurant I can take my daughter to, although reading a book is out of the question these days. Trinco is an all-day, vegetarian Tamil Sri Lankan restaurant founded by Vibushan Thirukumar, whose family moved to the UK during the Sri Lankan civil war. The food is knockout. For lunch, it’s all about the beautiful Marsala bean paratha wraps with chutney and green chilli; by night it’s all about a selection of rotis and curries made with seasonal vegetables. I’m in awe of restaurants that are predominantly vegan, as you have to build so much flavour with far fewer options. Let’s be honest: it’s not hard to make a steak delicious with the holy trinity of butter, cream and cheese. So top marks to Trinco for super-creative and delicious cooking. Open Monday-Wednesday, 8am-7pm; Thursday-Friday, 8am-10pm; Saturday, 9am-10pm; Sunday, 9am-7pm. Website; Directions Zeret Kitchen (Camberwell) Camberwell is one of the most interesting food neighbourhoods in the UK, let alone south London. You’ve got cult favourite Xinjiang restaurant Silk Road, some of the best pizza in London (Theo’s), definitely the best bakery in London (Toad) and one of only two Michelin-starred pubs in London (The Kerfield Arms). But for me, the restaurant that needs more attention is Zeret Kitchen. This buzzy Ethiopian spot is a place to gather around an enormous silver platter of injera with any number of combinations. The injera is baked thin and springy, with just the right amount of sour ferment to pair perfectly with the (often vegan) stews. My ultimate Camberwell itinerary would start at Zeret Kitchen and end with a show at Jazzlive at the Crypt, under St Giles Church. This jazz institution has been going since 1995 and many of my earliest memories as a kid were watching my jazz musician father play here until the early hours. Open Monday and Wednesday-Friday, 5.30pm-11pm; Saturday-Sunday, 1pm-11pm. Website; Directions James Dye is the co-founder of The Knave of Clubs, One Club Row and Bambi Which restaurant is your go-to in south London? Tell us in the comments below.
